transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Narang (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (CTO, ArgusWorks), Lena Morris (Lead ML Engineer), Tom Alvarez (Security Manager)

Summary: quick discovery to understand TTFT (time-to-first-token) expectations, free credits for PLG onramp, and evaluate whether ArgusWorks should start on Redwood Hosted or go straight to Dedicated/VPC pilot.

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, I'm the AE working with ArgusWorks. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Samir (ArgusWorks CTO): Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to see the onramp options.
[00:10] Lena (Lead ML Eng): Hi all. Wanted to be on this call to talk tech constraints — latency, token costs, and what you recommend for a pilot.
[00:18] Tom (Security): And I'll mostly focus on security, S O C two requirements, K M S, and where data lives.

[00:25] Jordan: Great. High level, we'll run through the PLG self-serve path — free credits, how quickly you can get to first token, then dive into hosted vs dedicated vs private given your constraints. Priya will talk about performance and recommended configs.

[01:02] Priya (Redwood SE): Quick intro from me — I work on inference optim and deployments. We'll cover batching, K V cache behavior, and quantization suggestions. Also we'll show what a dedicated GPU pool looks like compared to hosted.

[01:30] Samir: Cool. Our primary workload is a vector search + summarization pipeline for internal docs and some customer-facing snippets. Peak QPS is modest right now — maybe 50 requests/sec, but those are bursty. Latency today target is sub-300ms for 90th perc. Cost is important too; we can't blow up ops spend.

[02:05] Jordan: Useful. That 50 RPS bursty pattern is a classic fit for either hosted with autoscaling or Dedicated with reserved capacity plus burst. Hosted gives fastest TTFT — you sign up, we provision an account and you can do your first call within minutes using free credits. Dedicated gives predictable tail latency under load but requires a short provisioning lead time.

[02:42] Lena: When you say "first call within minutes" — what's involved? Do we need to upload models? SDKs? Can our engineers be calling from CI in the same day?

[02:55] Jordan: Yes. The PLG path: sign up, receive free credits, API key in the console, follow quickstart — we've got SDKs (Python/Node), example curl. Most teams hit their first token in under an hour; typical TTFT for experienced devs is 10-20 minutes. We'll provision a trial quota so you won't hit rate limits.

[03:30] Tom: From a security lens, if we go hosted, what are the guarantees around logs, retention, and K M S? We need audit logs and an option to integrate with our KMS for encryption at rest ideally.

[03:48] Priya: Hosted supports customer-controlled KMS for private deployments, but for the hosted public API we support encryption in transit and at rest managed by Redwood with SOC2 compliance. We have a private offering — Redwood Private — that gives you a VPC control plane and optional bring-your-own-KMS/HSM. I'll share our SOC2 + ISO docs after the call.

[04:20] Samir: If we start on hosted for speed, could we move to Dedicated later without code changes? Migrations are a headache for us.

[04:32] Priya: That's a core design point — same API surface. You can pin model versions and rollout policies. Switching routing from hosted pool to a dedicated capacity is a config change; no code rewrite needed. We do recommend running a smoke test when you migrate to verify latency and token accounting match your expectations.

[05:05] Lena: What's the difference in cost per token on hosted vs dedicated? Ballpark numbers are fine.

[05:12] Jordan: I'll send the formal sheet, but ballpark: hosted is usage-based with published per-token rates and embedding prices. Dedicated is a reserved capacity model: you buy a pool (monthly) that gives you a predictable per-token cost when fully utilized; effective cost depends on utilization. For bursty low-utilization workloads hosted often wins on raw dollar spend, but dedicated gives consistent latency and sometimes lower cost at scale.

[05:50] Tom: We have to present options to procurement. They will ask for SOC2, ISO, SAML SSO, and audit log details. Also any third-party subprocessors.

[06:05] Jordan: Understood. Action: I'll email SOC2/ISO and a security one-pager. Also we'll include SAML/SSO configuration steps.

[06:20] Priya: Back to the workload: for search + summarization, caching matters. Redwood's prefix caching and K V cache can cut downstream tokens significantly if you have repeated context. There are also continuous batching benefits for throughput but that can add a bit of latency . We typically suggest conservative batching for low-latency use-cases.

[07:00] Samir: Can you quantify the latency impact of batching? We need 90th percentile under 300 ms.

[07:10] Priya: On dedicated with a well-tuned pipeline and small batch sizes you'll see p90 around 150-250ms for <1k token requests on modern GPU configs. On hosted it varies by the model and noisy neighbor effects but we've got protections and prioritization for paid customers. For strict p90 under 300ms, Dedicated is less risky.

[07:45] Lena: What about model quantization? We want to squeeze cost but keep summarization quality.

[07:53] Priya: We recommend mixed precision or 4-bit quant for many workloads — we have model recommendations per workload in the Optimize tooling. We'll attach sample evals that compare quality drop vs token savings. For extractive summarization, losses are usually small.

[08:25] Speaker 3: (transcription glitch) "red wood re-route" — I think they meant routing policies.

[08:35] Jordan: Good callout. Also, on the PLG credits: we'll provision 30 days of free credits that should be enough to run smoke tests and a small benchmark. It's not for production but enough to validate integration and perf. After the credit expires you can either pay-as-you-go or negotiate a dedicated pilot.

[09:05] Samir: How do you recommend we benchmark? We'll want end-to-end numbers including our pre/post processing.

[09:15] Priya: Best practice: provide a representative sample of payloads (we'll accept gzipped batches), and we'll run three profiles: latency tail under steady-state, burst ramp tests to simulate 50 RPS bursts, and an embedding throughput test. We'll return results in a spreadsheet with token counts and cost estimates.

[09:50] Lena: Can we run those tests against both hosted and a dedicated staging cluster to compare?

[09:58] Priya: Yes, for Dedicated we can spin a short-lived reserved pool in a dedicated account for the pilot. It requires some lead time — usually 48-72 hours to fully provision and warm caches. Hosted tests can be immediate.

[10:25] Tom: For compliance: if we do Hosted pilot, will customer data be accessible by Redwood staff or subprocessors? We need an assurance on access levels.

[10:38] Jordan: Access to customer data is restricted; we use role-based access controls and audit logs. For higher assurance customers we offer private deployments with customer-managed VPC and KMS so Redwood staff cannot access keys. I'll include the data access section from our security doc.

[11:00] Samir: Great. A couple of tactical questions — do you have client libraries that do automatic retry/backoff, token accounting, and streaming?

[11:10] Jordan: Yes. Python and Node SDKs include retry/backoff, streaming chunks, function-calling transforms, and per-request token metadata. We also expose a console with token-level cost breakdowns.

[11:40] Lena: Any limits on sequence length or memory for KV caches? We're often sending 2-3k tokens of context.

[11:50] Priya: We support long-context variants; limits depend on model. For 2–3k tokens it's fine but you should choose a model profile that's optimized for medium-length sequences. The K V cache will help when you do incremental generation — note though that K V cache is per-session so be mindful of session affinity for cache hits.

[12:20] Samir: You mentioned session affinity — is that supported across a dedicated pool split across nodes?

[12:28] Priya: Yes, we have a placement and affinity layer. For Dedicated we route to the right node for warm KV hits. For hosted it's probabilistic but the platform does sticky routing heuristics for cache warmness. There are edge cases where a cold start will miss K V state and add latency; we document warmup strategies.

[13:00] Jordan: Quick commercial check — what's your timeline to decide?

[13:07] Samir: We'd like to run a pilot in 3–4 weeks and decide by end of Q2. Procurement review will likely take 2 weeks once we have the SOC2 docs and pricing.

[13:20] Jordan: Sounds doable. We'll aim to get docs and pricing to you within 48 hours and provision credits the next day.

[13:35] Lena: On the pilot, can we test a quantized model and an unquantized one to compare quality?

[13:42] Priya: Absolutely. We'll recommend a few model variants — one FP16 and one 4-bit quant — and run identical inputs through both. We'll provide evaluation metrics (ROUGE, embedding similarity) so you can judge quality drop.

[14:10] Tom: For the dedicated option, what SLAs do you provide for uptime and latency?

[14:18] Jordan: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and response time targets in the contract. Exact numbers depend on the reserved capacity tier; I can include the SLA table in the pricing sheet.

[14:35] Samir: One gotcha we had with other vendors is price surprises from tokenization differences and system messages. How do you recommend we avoid surprise bills?

[14:47] Priya: We provide token accounting in the console and token-level cost breakdowns per request. Also Optimize tooling suggests prompt engineering to cut token use, and you can set quotas & alerts to avoid surprises. We'll share a sample cost analysis template.

[15:10] Jordan: Any competitors you're evaluating?

[15:14] Samir: Yeah, we're looking at Anthropic for safety features, OpenAI for ease-of-use, and evaluating SageMaker endpoints internally. Also a couple of smaller infra vendors like Replicate.

[15:30] Jordan: Noted. We can emphasize our migration story, private deployments, and cost controls in follow-ups.

[15:45] Lena: One more operational question — how do you handle model version rollouts? If you pin a model and we want to roll forward, can we do canary tests?

[15:55] Priya: Yes, rollouts support canary traffic slices and automatic fallback to previous versions if quality/regression alerts trigger. It's configurable per-route.

[16:15] Samir: About data residency — we have EU customers; do you have region-specific hosting?

[16:22] Jordan: Yes, we have multi-region options and can pin deployments to regions. For Private or Dedicated we can ensure the compute is in your desired region.

[16:40] Tom: SSO — do you support SAML and SCIM for provisioning?

[16:45] Jordan: Yes, both SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported for enterprise accounts. We'll include the step-by-step in the follow-up.

[17:00] Samir: Ok, sounds like a plan. Two things for us: 1) we'll share a small sample set of real requests and expected throughput; 2) procurement will want pricing and SOC2 docs.

[17:10] Jordan: We'll act on both. Priya will take the sample payloads and schedule the benchmark run. Jordan will send the security + pricing.

[17:25] Priya: For the benchmark, please include typical payload sizes and a separate file for expected concurrency patterns. We'll run hosted tests immediately and start Dedicated provisioning once you confirm that's desired.

[17:45] Lena: What's a good way to validate quality across quantized models? We use a mix of ROUGE and manual human review.

[17:55] Priya: Combine automatic metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, embedding similarity) with a small human review set. We'll return both numbers and sample responses to help you decide.

[18:20] Speaker 2: (brief cross-talk) "yeah, yeah"

[18:35] Jordan: Okay — recap of next steps: I'll send docs and provision credits; Priya will coordinate benchmarks; Samir will share payloads and QPS patterns; Tom will give a short list of security questions to answer. We'll schedule the technical deep dive for the week of April 13th.

[19:02] Samir: That timeline works. Any blockers from your side?

[19:08] Jordan: None on our side. We'll get the paperwork and account set up quickly.

[19:15] Tom: Quick question — in case we need on-prem air-gapped deployment, is that possible?

[19:22] Priya: We do offer an on-prem package for high-compliance customers. It's heavier lift and typically for later-stage enterprise deals; we can discuss prerequisites in the deep dive.

[19:40] Lena: One last small thing — do you support streaming for partial results? We have UI needs for progressive rendering.

[19:46] Jordan: Yes, streaming is supported in the API and SDKs. We'll include an example of chunked responses.

[20:00] Samir: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the sample payloads and procurement questions.

[20:10] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll send the security doc and pricing by Tuesday and set up credits. Priya will be in touch about bench requests.

[20:22] (call ends; remaining time used for casual scheduling chat)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (S O C two / SAM L) and speaker attribution occasionally generic. Overall medium quality auto transcript.
